mainTopic: אדמון's disputes with the חכמים: sons and daughters sharing a small estate, and a claim for jugs of oil where only the jugs are admitted.
overview: The amud opens with the last lines of an earlier discussion: a borrower's shame before his lender counts as something he benefits from being freed of. Then a new משנה lists disputes of אדמון. In the first, sons inherit a large estate while daughters are fed from it, but from a small estate only the daughters are fed. אדמון protests, 'Because I am a male, I lose?' and רבן גמליאל agrees. אביי says אדמון is pointing to the male's Torah learning. רבא rejects that and explains that the heir of a large estate should not lose everything in a small one. The next משנה is about someone who claims jugs of oil while the other admits only to the jugs. אדמון requires an oath, and חכמים exempt him. The גמרא tests several readings against rulings of שמואל and רבי חייא בר אבא. It concludes that the argument is whether 'ten jugs of oil' includes the jugs, in a case where the oil is denied and five jugs are admitted. The amud ends as a third משנה begins, about a father-in-law who promised a dowry and went bankrupt.

steps.title: Doesn't the borrower feel shame?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the earlier comparison. Doesn't the person in debt feel shame?
steps.simpleTranslation: Doesn't he have shame?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the discussion from the previous section. It challenges a comparison by pointing out that a borrower feels embarrassed in front of his lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that a debtor does lose something real: his comfort, because he is embarrassed until the debt is paid. If that shame counts, then removing it is a real benefit, and the comparison has to account for it.

phrases.english: Doesn't he have shame?
phrases.notes: 'He' is the person who owes the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier comparison, which ignored the debtor's shame
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A debtor's embarrassment is a real loss, so ending it should count.

steps.title: Being freed from shame counts as benefit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in the other case too, the person has a benefit: he is freed from the shame he feels before his lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too he has benefit: that benefit of being ashamed before him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. In the other case too, the shame a borrower feels counts as something he benefits from getting rid of.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer agrees that shame matters. It says the shame is present in the other case as well. So paying off the debt removes the embarrassment, and that counts as a real הנאה (benefit) there too.

keyTerms.meaning: That he is ashamed before him

phrases.english: There too he has benefit,
that benefit of being ashamed before him.
phrases.notes: He means that getting rid of the embarrassment of owing money is itself the benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the same factor exists in both cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think shame only matters in one case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Removing a debtor's shame counts as real benefit in the other case too.
steps.whatToRemember: A debtor's embarrassment before his lender counts. Removing it is a real הנאה.

steps.title: The rule: large estate vs. small estate
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה begins with אדמון's seven disputes. The first case: sons inherit a large estate and daughters are fed from it. With a small estate, the daughters are fed and the sons must go begging.
steps.simpleTranslation: אדמון disagrees in seven cases. If a man dies and leaves sons and daughters: when the estate is large, the sons inherit and the daughters are fed. When the estate is small, the daughters are fed and the sons go around to the doors.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts here. It lists cases where אדמון disagrees with the חכמים. The first case lays out the standard rule for dividing a father's estate between sons and daughters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law, sons inherit. Daughters have the right to be supported from the estate. When there is enough for both, everyone is covered. When there isn't enough, the daughters' support comes first, so the sons may be left with nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא (sage of the משנה) who was a judge in ירושלים
A small estate, not enough for both sons and daughters
They go around to the doors, meaning they beg

steps.confusionAlert: In a small estate, the daughters do NOT inherit. They are only fed and supported. The sons are still the legal heirs, but nothing is left for them.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Admon states seven:
phrases.notes: There are seven cases where אדמון disagrees with the חכמים. This is the first one.

phrases.english: One who died and left sons and daughters,
when the estate is large,
the sons inherit, and the daughters are fed.
And with a small estate, the daughters are fed,
and the sons go around to the doors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A brand-new topic: the start of a new משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Large estate: sons inherit and daughters are fed. Small estate: daughters are fed and sons get nothing.

steps.title: אדמון protests: Should I lose because I'm male?
steps.stepSummary: אדמון objects to the small-estate rule: should the son lose out just because he is a male?
steps.simpleTranslation: אדמון says: Because I am a male, I lose?!
steps.whatsHappening: אדמון disagrees with the rule we just learned. He speaks as if he were the son and protests that being male leaves him with nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אדמון finds it unfair that the son, who is the actual heir, ends up worse off than the daughters. His exact reasoning is unclear, and the גמרא asks about it in step 6.

phrases.english: Admon says:
Because I am a male, I lose out?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְמוֹן אוֹמֵר: בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאֲנִי זָכָר הִפְסַדְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the small-estate rule in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that sons get nothing from a small estate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being male should not make the son worse off than the daughters.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל sides with אדמון
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל says he agrees with אדמון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל said: I see the words of אדמון as correct.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל gives his opinion and says that אדמון is right. This closes the משנה's first case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With רבן גמליאל's agreement, אדמון's view gains real weight against the standard rule. רבן גמליאל only agrees here; he does not add a new reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Head of the סנהדרין, a leading תנא
I see as correct the words of

phrases.english: Rabban Gamliel said:
I see the words of Admon as correct.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אַדְמוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Agrees with אדמון's protest in step 4.
steps.whatToRemember: The basic rule: daughters are fed first from a small estate. אדמון objects, and רבן גמליאל agrees with him.

steps.title: What does אדמון mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what אדמון's argument actually is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks what אדמון meant by 'because I am a male.' This sets up the two explanations that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being male is exactly why the son loses in a small estate, so it is unclear how that fact can be his argument. The גמרא needs to know what is special about being male that should protect him.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is he saying?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the meaning of אדמון's words in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the logic behind אדמון's 'because I am a male'?

steps.title: אביי: Because I can learn Torah
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that אדמון means: I am a male who is fit to learn Torah. Should I be the one to lose?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said, this is what he means: Because I am a male and fit to learn Torah, I lose out?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. He says אדמון is pointing to the son's ability to learn Torah, which makes it wrong for him to be left with nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אביי's reading, being male stands for being able to devote oneself to Torah. Leaving such a person to beg seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Fit to engage in Torah learning

phrases.english: Abaye said, this is what he is saying:
Because I am a male
and fit to engage in Torah, I lose out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אדמון is pointing to the male's ability to learn Torah.

steps.title: רבא: Inheritance doesn't depend on Torah learning
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects אביי's reading: inheritance has nothing to do with whether someone learns Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Is it only one who learns Torah who inherits, and one who doesn't learn Torah doesn't inherit?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's explanation. Torah learning has no connection to the laws of inheritance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אביי were right, a son who does not learn would have no complaint at all. But the inheritance laws treat every son the same, so Torah learning cannot be the point of אדמון's argument.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Is it one who engages in Torah who inherits,

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּלָא עָסֵיק בַּתּוֹרָה לָא יָרֵית?!
phrases.english: and one who does not engage in Torah does not inherit?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: מַאן דְּעָסֵיק בַּתּוֹרָה הוּא דְּיָרֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's answer in step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inheritance rights do not depend on Torah learning, so that cannot be אדמון's reason.

steps.title: רבא: The heir of a large estate shouldn't lose a small one
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that אדמון means: I am the legal heir of a large estate, so how can I lose everything in a small one?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said, this is what he means: Because I am a male and fit to inherit a large estate, I lose out in a small estate?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own explanation of אדמון. The son's argument comes from his status as the Torah's heir.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a large estate, the son's rights are stronger than the daughters', because he inherits and they are only fed. אדמון argues that it makes no sense for the stronger right to turn into nothing when the estate is small. The argument is built entirely on inheritance law, so it avoids the problem רבא raised against אביי.
steps.whatToRemember: אדמון's complaint, as רבא reads it: if the son's rights beat the daughters' in a large estate, how can he lose everything in a small one?

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said, this is what he is saying:
Because I am a male
and fit to inherit a large estate,
I lose out in a small estate?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's answer after the attack in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אדמון argues that the son's stronger inheritance rights in a large estate should not disappear in a small estate.

steps.title: New משנה: Claiming jugs of oil, admitting only to the jugs
steps.stepSummary: Someone claims jugs of oil, and the other admits only to the jugs. אדמון requires an oath. חכמים say the admission is a different kind than the claim. רבן גמליאל agrees with אדמון.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone claims his friend owes him jugs of oil, and the friend admits only to the jugs, אדמון says: since he admitted to part of the claim, he must swear. חכמים say: this partial admission is not the same kind of thing as the claim. רבן גמליאל said: I agree with אדמון.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts here. It brings a new case where אדמון and חכמים argue about a partial admission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, someone who admits to part of a claim (מודה במקצת) must swear about the rest. אדמון treats admitting to the jugs as part of the claim of 'jugs of oil.' חכמים say jugs are not the same kind of thing as oil, so there is no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes a claim against someone
One who admits to part of a claim, and so must swear about the rest
The same type of thing as what was claimed

steps.confusionAlert: 'Jugs of oil' can mean two different things: the oil together with the jugs, or just an amount of oil. The גמרא is about to argue over which one the משנה means.
steps.whyThisMatters: The case tests a basic rule of oaths. Does admitting to something connected to the claim, but different from it, count as a partial admission?

phrases.english: MISHNA
One who claims from his fellow jugs of oil
and the other admitted to the pitchers
Admon says
since he admitted to part of the claim
he must swear
And the Rabbis say
the partial admission is not of the same type as the claim
Rabban Gamliel said
I see the words of Admon as correct

steps.triggerLanguage: הַטּוֹעֵן אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ כַּדֵּי שֶׁמֶן וְהוֹדָה בַּקַּנְקַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה with another dispute between אדמון and חכמים, where רבן גמליאל again sides with אדמון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדמון: admitting to the jugs counts as a partial admission, so he must swear. חכמים: the admission is a different kind than the claim, so there is no oath.

steps.title: Learning from חכמים: admitting to barley out of a wheat-and-barley claim is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a rule from חכמים. If someone claims wheat and barley and the other admits only to the barley, he is exempt from an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: We can learn from חכמים: if he claimed wheat and barley and the other admitted to the barley, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a general rule out of the opinion of חכמים in the משנה. It understands the claim as being for both the oil and the jugs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the claim was for oil and jugs, then admitting to the jugs is admitting to one of the two items claimed. חכמים still exempt him from an oath. So the same should apply to any claim for two items, like wheat and barley, where he admits to only one.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this; we can conclude from here

phrases.english: GEMARA
Conclude from here, according to the Rabbis
if he claimed from him wheat and barley
and he admitted to the barley
he is exempt
phrases.notes: Just like the jugs-of-oil case, where admitting only to the jugs brings no oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the opinion of חכמים in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to חכמים, claiming two kinds of items and admitting to only one kind brings no oath.

steps.title: Does this refute רב נחמן in the name of שמואל?
steps.stepSummary: The rule drawn from חכמים seems to contradict רב נחמן in the name of שמואל. He says that admitting to one of wheat and barley does require an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this refutes רב נחמן in the name of שמואל? For רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: if he claimed wheat and barley and the other admitted to one of them, he is obligated to swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the הלכה of רב נחמן in the name of שמואל. Its ruling looks like the exact opposite of what we just learned from חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 learned from חכמים that admitting to one of two claimed items means no oath. רב נחמן in the name of שמואל rules that the same admission does bring an oath. So an אמורא's ruling seems to contradict the חכמים of the משנה, and that looks like a refutation.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion, often a challenge)
A refutation that knocks down an opinion

phrases.english: Shall we say this is a refutation
of what Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel?
For Rav Nachman said in the name of Shmuel
if he claimed from him wheat and barley
and he admitted to him one of them
he is obligated to swear

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא תִּהְוֵי תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּרַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the rule from step 11 to challenge a ruling of an אמורא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of רב נחמן in the name of שמואל that admitting to one of two claimed items requires an oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: חכמים in the משנה exempt someone who admits to one of two claimed items (oil and jugs). שמואל obligates him in the same kind of case, so he seems to contradict חכמים.

steps.title: The claim was only for an amount of oil
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב explains that the משנה's claimant asked only for a measure of oil, not for jugs at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: the משנה is talking about where he claimed a measure (an amount of oil).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the משנה differently. The claim was only for oil, measured in jugs, and never for the jugs themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the claim was only for oil, then the jugs were never part of the claim at all. Admitting to the jugs is admitting to something that was not claimed, so חכמים exempt him. This says nothing about a claim for two items like wheat and barley, so שמואל is not refuted.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure; an amount (of oil that fills a certain number of jugs)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav
It is where he claimed from him a measure
phrases.notes: He means 'jugs of oil' was just a way to say how much oil, not a claim for the jugs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב בְּטוֹעֲנוֹ מִדָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the refutation in step 12 by redefining the case in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא) of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The claim in the משנה was for both oil and jugs, so חכמים exempt someone who admits to one of two claimed items.
steps.terutzMaskana: The claim was only for an amount of oil. The jugs were never claimed, so the משנה does not conflict with שמואל's wheat-and-barley ruling.

steps.title: If so, why does אדמון require an oath?
steps.stepSummary: Once the claim is only for oil, it is hard to see why אדמון would treat admitting to the jugs as a partial admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the reason of אדמון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading from step 13. If the jugs were never claimed, how can אדמון say admitting to them requires an oath?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 13 explains the view of חכמים well, but it causes trouble for אדמון. If the claim was only for oil, admitting to the jugs is about something completely different. So it is unclear why אדמון calls it a partial admission.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is the case

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה is being read as a claim for only an amount of oil. That explains the view of חכמים and saves שמואל, but it leaves אדמון's view needing an explanation.

phrases.english: If so
what is the reason of Admon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading in step 13 because of how it affects אדמון's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reading that the claim in the משנה was only for a measure of oil.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the jugs were never claimed, admitting to them cannot be part of the claim. So אדמון's ruling that he must swear seems to have no basis.

steps.title: רבא's new approach: two cases everyone agrees on
steps.stepSummary: רבא sets aside the earlier answer. He explains that 'a full ten jugs of oil in your pit' is a claim for oil only, while 'ten full jugs of oil with you' is a claim for both oil and jugs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: Everyone agrees that if he said 'I have the fill of ten jugs of oil in your pit,' he is claiming only oil, not jugs. If he said 'I have ten full jugs of oil with you,' he is claiming both the oil and the jugs.
steps.whatsHappening: Since Step 14 showed a problem with רב יהודה's answer, רבא offers a different answer. He starts by laying out two cases where אדמון and חכמים would agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording of the claim decides what is being claimed. 'The fill of ten jugs' is just a way of measuring oil, so admitting to jugs has nothing to do with the claim. 'Ten full jugs' names the jugs themselves, so admitting to the jugs is admitting to part of the claim, and everyone agrees an oath is required.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who gives the new answer here
A pit, used here to store oil

steps.confusionAlert: The two phrasings sound almost the same. 'מלא עשרה כדי שמן' means 'the amount that fills ten jugs,' so it is about oil only. 'עשרה כדי שמן מלאים' means 'ten jugs that are full,' so it is about the jugs too.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
phrases.notes: 'Rather' means רבא is dropping רב יהודה's answer from Step 13 and offering a new one.

phrases.english: Everyone agrees that
where he said to him:
'The fill of ten jugs of oil'
'I have in your pit,'
he is claiming oil from him,
he is not claiming jugs from him.
'Ten full jugs of oil'
'I have with you' —
he is claiming oil and jugs from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב יהודה's answer after the challenge in Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reading of the case in the משנה, based on how the claim is worded
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The claim in the משנה was only for a measure of oil, which made אדמון's view hard to explain
steps.terutzMaskana: Two clearly worded cases are agreed upon. The argument must be about some other wording.

steps.title: Where אדמון and the רבנן disagree: the unclear wording
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about the plain phrase 'ten jugs of oil.' אדמון says it includes the jugs, and רבנן say it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree when he said 'I have ten jugs of oil with you.' אדמון says this wording includes the jugs. רבנן hold that it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his answer by pinning down the exact case of the argument in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is now only about what the words mean, not about the law of partial admission. If the phrase includes jugs, as אדמון says, admitting to the jugs is a partial admission. If it does not, as רבנן say, admitting to the jugs is about something that was never claimed.

keyTerms.meaning: A judge whose rulings are recorded in this פרק
The Rabbis (the חכמים of the משנה)

steps.whyThisMatters: This moves the whole argument from a question of law to a question of how people speak, which sets up the challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: When they disagree
is where he said to him:
'I have ten jugs of oil with you.'
phrases.notes: Notice there is no 'full' and no 'fill of' here. That is why the meaning is unclear.

phrases.english: Admon says:
this expression includes a reference to jugs,
and the Rabbis hold:
this expression does not include a reference to jugs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's answer by naming the case they argue about
steps.terutzResolutionType: Puts the argument in the meaning of the words
steps.terutzMaskana: אדמון and רבנן argue only about whether 'ten jugs of oil' includes the jugs

steps.title: רבא's reading seems to clash with רבי חייא בר אבא
steps.stepSummary: From רבא's reading, it follows that if the wording did include jugs, רבנן would require an oath. That seems to go against רבי חייא בר אבא, who says that admitting to one of two claimed items (wheat and barley) brings no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the only reason רבנן exempt him is that the wording does not include jugs. That means if it did include jugs, he would have to swear. Should we say this refutes רבי חייא בר אבא? He said: if someone claimed wheat and barley and the other admitted to one of them, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from רבא's answer and uses it to challenge a ruling of רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבא, oil and jugs are two different items. If both were claimed and only the jugs were admitted, רבנן would still require an oath. That matches רב נחמן's view and goes against רבי חייא בר אבא, who exempts someone who admits to only one of two different items.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggested conclusion)

steps.confusionAlert: In Steps 11–12, reading רבנן led to 'exempt,' which clashed with רב נחמן. Now רבא's reading leads to 'obligated,' which clashes with רבי חייא בר אבא. The clash has switched sides.

phrases.english: But then, the reason is
that this expression does not include a reference to jugs,

phrases.aramaic: הָא יֵשׁ בַּלָּשׁוֹן הַזֶּה לְשׁוֹן קַנְקַנִּים — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: so if the expression did include a reference to jugs, he would be obligated.
Shall we say this is a refutation
of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba?
For Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said:
If he claimed wheat and barley from him
and he admitted to one of them, he is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא תֶּיהְוֵי תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from רבא's answer and challenges it
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא בר אבא's ruling that admitting to one of two different items brings no oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under רבא, רבנן would require an oath when someone admits to the jugs out of a claim for oil and jugs, which are two different items. That goes against רבי חייא בר אבא's exemption.

steps.title: רב שימי בר אשי: oil in jugs is like a pomegranate in its peel
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי answers that oil and its jugs are not two separate items like wheat and barley. They are one unit, like a pomegranate with its peel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: It is as if he claimed a pomegranate in its peel.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי defends רבי חייא בר אבא by showing that the oil case is different from the wheat-and-barley case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא בר אבא's exemption covers two unconnected items. Oil and the jugs holding it are joined together, like fruit and its peel, so admitting to the jugs is admitting to part of one item. In that case even רבי חייא בר אבא would agree an oath is required.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who answers the challenge

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
It is as if he claimed from him
a pomegranate in its peel.
phrases.notes: The jugs are like the peel and the oil is like the fruit inside, so together they count as one thing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: נַעֲשָׂה כְּמִי שֶׁטְּעָנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבי חייא בר אבא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the cases are different: oil and jugs are one unit, not two separate items
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Oil and jugs are two separate items, like wheat and barley
steps.terutzMaskana: Oil in jugs is one item, like a pomegranate in its peel, so רבי חייא בר אבא's exemption does not apply

steps.title: רבינא: oil can survive without its jugs
steps.stepSummary: רבינא rejects the comparison. A pomegranate cannot be kept without its peel, but oil can be kept without these particular jugs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא objected: A pomegranate without its peel does not keep, but oil does keep without jugs!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks רב שימי בר אשי's comparison and shows it does not hold up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The peel is needed for the pomegranate to last, so the two really are one unit. Oil can be poured into any other container, so the jugs are a separate item. That brings back the clash with רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא: everyone agrees on 'the fill of ten jugs' (oil only) and on 'ten full jugs' (oil and jugs). The argument is only about 'ten jugs of oil.' This seems to clash with רבי חייא בר אבא. רב שימי בר אשי compares it to a pomegranate in its peel, and רבינא answers that oil, unlike a pomegranate, keeps without its container.

phrases.english: Ravina objected to it:
A pomegranate without its peel does not keep,
but oil keeps without jugs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison given in Step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שימי בר אשי's comparison of oil in jugs to a pomegranate in its peel
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A peel is needed to keep a pomegranate, so the two are one unit. Jugs are not needed to keep oil, so oil and jugs stay two separate items.

steps.title: A new case: the oil is denied completely, and only some of the jugs are admitted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives up its earlier picture and sets up a new case. The defendant denies the oil completely but admits to five of the ten jugs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here is the case. One person said, 'I have ten jugs of oil with you.' The other answered, 'The oil never happened. As for the jugs, you have five with me, and five you do not have.'
steps.whatsHappening: Because רבינא knocked down the pomegranate answer, the גמרא now describes a different case to explain the dispute. This step only sets up the case; the next steps explain how אדמון and the רבנן rule on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the problem was that oil and jugs looked like two separate items, like wheat and barley. In this new case, the defendant admits nothing about the oil. He admits only to part of the jugs, so whatever he admits is the same kind of item he partly denies. That avoids the wheat-and-barley problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with? (introduces a new description of the case)
These things never happened (a full denial)

steps.confusionAlert: In the earlier steps the defendant also admitted to the jugs, not the oil. What is new here is that he admits only five of the ten jugs. So his admission is part of the jug claim itself, not one item out of two separate items.

phrases.english: Rather, here what are we dealing with?
A case where one said to the other:

phrases.aramaic: עֲשָׂרָה כַּדֵּי שֶׁמֶן יֵשׁ לִי אֶצְלְךָ,
phrases.english: I have ten jugs of oil with you,
and the other said to him:
The oil: it never happened;
as for the jugs, five you do have with me,
and five you do not have.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבינא's rejection in step 19 by describing a new case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute was about a defendant who admitted to the jugs out of a claim for oil and jugs. That looked like admitting one of two separate items, like wheat and barley.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is about a defendant who denies the oil completely and admits to only some of the jugs.

steps.title: אדמון's reasoning: the jug oath pulls in the oil
steps.stepSummary: אדמון holds that the phrase includes the jugs. So the defendant owes an oath on the jugs, and through גלגול he must also swear about the oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: אדמון says: this wording includes a claim for the jugs. Since he must swear about the jugs, he must also swear about the oil, by rolling it into the same oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how אדמון rules in the new case. Because the claim covered the jugs, the defendant admitted part of the claim and must swear, and the oil gets added on to that oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting five jugs out of ten claimed is a real partial admission of the same item, so it requires an oath. Once an oath is required, the claimant can 'roll' other claims into it. That is how the completely denied oil also becomes part of the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Since (here: since he already has to do one thing, he must do another)
By 'rolling': adding another claim onto an oath he already owes

steps.whyThisMatters: This is where גלגול שבועה comes in. On its own, a full denial of the oil would not bring an oath, but it gets pulled into the oath he already owes.

phrases.english: Admon says:
This wording includes a claim for jugs,
and since he must swear about the jugs,

phrases.aramaic: מִשְׁתְּבַע נָמֵי אַשֶּׁמֶן עַל יְדֵי גִּלְגּוּל.
phrases.english: he swears about the oil as well, by rolling it in.
phrases.notes: Rolling in means that once he owes one oath, other claims can be added to that same oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְמוֹן אוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ בַּלָּשׁוֹן הַזֶּה לְשׁוֹן קַנְקַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies אדמון's view to the case set up in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying the new case to the first opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed that an oath here would mean an oath for admitting one of two separate items.
steps.terutzMaskana: For אדמון, the oath comes from a partial admission of the jugs themselves, and the oil is added through גלגול.

steps.title: The רבנן's reasoning: the claim and the admission don't match
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that the phrase does not include the jugs. So the defendant denied everything that was claimed, and what he admitted was never claimed. No oath is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן hold: this wording does not include a claim for jugs. What he was claimed, he did not admit, and what he admitted, he was not claimed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the רבנן's side of the new case. This finishes the explanation of the whole dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim was only for oil, and the oil was fully denied. The jugs were admitted, but they were never claimed. Since nothing was partly admitted, there is no oath to begin with, and nothing can be rolled into one.
steps.whatToRemember: Everything depends on what the phrase 'ten jugs of oil' means. If it includes the jugs (אדמון), there is a partial admission and an oath, with the oil rolled in. If it means oil only (רבנן), the claim and the admission don't overlap, so there is no oath.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold:
This wording does not include a claim for jugs.
What he claimed from him, he did not admit to him,
phrases.notes: That's the oil: it was claimed but fully denied.

phrases.english: and what he admitted to him, he had not claimed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: אֵין בַּלָּשׁוֹן הַזֶּה לְשׁוֹן קַנְקַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the dispute in the case from step 20 and closes the discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The dispute between אדמון and the רבנן is about whether 'ten jugs of oil' includes the jugs. That decides whether admitting to the jugs creates an oath that pulls in the oil.

steps.title: New משנה: a man promises money to his son-in-law and then goes broke
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה opens with another case involving אדמון. A man promised his son-in-law a sum of money and then went bankrupt.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who promised money to his son-in-law, and then 'stretched out his leg' (went bankrupt)...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new משנה. Only the setup of the case appears here; the ruling continues in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic moves from oath claims to a promised dowry that the father-in-law can no longer pay. This משנה contains another ruling of אדמון, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
One who sets a fixed amount he promises to give
Literally 'stretched out his leg': went bankrupt

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who promises money to his son-in-law,
and then went bankrupt —
phrases.notes: The words literally say 'stretched out his leg.' It's an expression for going broke.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the oil-and-jugs discussion is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case of a father-in-law who promised a dowry and then went bankrupt. The ruling follows in the continuation.
